Phones and the Driver's Seat

Almost everyone I know carries a phone, and almost everyone I know has looked at it while driving. I have done it too, at a red light, telling myself it did not count because the car was not moving. That small excuse is the reason I think the rule should be simple: drivers should not handle a phone at all while operating a vehicle, and the only uses that should be allowed are ones that keep the hands on the wheel and the eyes on the road.

The main argument is about attention. Driving feels easy because most of the time nothing happens. A person can drive the same road to work for years without a single surprise. But the skill of driving is being ready for the one second when a child steps out between parked cars or the truck ahead brakes hard. Reading a text takes the eyes off the road for several seconds. At highway speed a car covers the length of a football field in about that time. The driver is not really driving during those seconds. The car is just moving on its own, and everyone nearby is trusting that nothing changes.

People often say they are good at multitasking, and I believed that about myself for a long time. The problem is that a driver who is distracted cannot notice what he misses. If I look down and nothing goes wrong, I conclude that I handled it fine. I never see the cyclist I would have hit on a different day. So each safe trip makes the habit stronger, and the confidence grows without any real evidence behind it. A law that bans handheld use takes that judgment away from the person least able to make it.

There is also the question of who pays for the mistake. If texting behind the wheel only endangered the person texting, I could see an argument for leaving it to personal choice. It does not work that way. The pedestrian in the crosswalk and the family in the next lane never agreed to the risk. We already accept this reasoning with drunk driving. Nobody argues that a driver has a right to decide for himself whether four beers affect him. A phone in the hand is a similar kind of impairment, and it is one that people choose over and over during a single trip.

I do not think the answer is a total ban on every function, though. Phones have replaced paper maps, and a navigation app that speaks directions aloud is probably safer than a lost driver squinting at street signs. Calling for help after a crash or reporting a dangerous driver is a good use too. A phone mounted on the dashboard, set up before the car leaves the driveway and controlled by voice, seems reasonable to me. Even hands-free calls take some attention away, so I would not call them harmless, but they are much easier to enforce a line around. An officer can see a phone in a hand. He cannot see a wandering mind.

So my position is that the phone should be set up before the trip starts and left alone until it ends. Messages can wait twenty minutes. If something truly cannot wait, the driver can pull over, which costs maybe two minutes. Compared with what can happen in the seconds spent looking down, that is a small price, and I think the law should make people pay it.
